strengths: The problem is well motivated. Figure 1 provides a clear analytic example where controlling X1 conditionally on C achieves expected reward 1/3, exceeding both unconditional interventions and jointly controlling all actionable variables.

Combining causal policy-scope reduction with contextual BO is a useful direction for continuous intervention problems. The modular algorithm and discussion of existing causal and contextual BO make the proposed approach understandable.

Experiments include cases where baseline policy classes can and cannot attain the optimum. Reporting 110 seeds, 700 iterations, and standard-error intervals provides useful evidence for the observed improvements on the selected synthetic environments.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to the cited work. The algorithm principally combines the existing POMPS characterization of Lee and Bareinboim, HEBO, and standard UCB. The manuscript provides neither a new structural result nor sufficient analysis or experimental evidence to establish this combination as a substantial advance over prior mixed-policy-scope learning.

The central scope-selection mechanism lacks adequate justification. Each arm's reward distribution changes as its BO learner improves, so standard stationary-bandit UCB reasoning does not directly apply. Section 4.2's observation that rewards become stationary at optimality assumes the outcome that needs establishing. No analysis controls this coupled learning process, and decreasing average regret over 700 iterations does not establish asymptotic sublinear regret or the conclusion's claim of always reaching the optimum.

Support for general mixed policy scopes is unclear. Definition 3.1 allows different information sets for different interventions, including contexts observed after earlier actions. Section 4 instead describes joint action optimization given a contextual vector. The manuscript needs to explain how Algorithm 1 respects observation timing and per-action information constraints; the experiments do not exercise these cases.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed UCB selector's contribution. In both PSA experiments, CoCa-BO has only one candidate POMPS, so its advantage cannot demonstrate better bandit selection. Missing controlled ablations include uniform allocation and acquisition-based selection where applicable, while holding candidate scopes and the inner BO implementation fixed. Much of the reported advantage establishes differences in policy-class expressiveness rather than selection efficiency.

Evaluation breadth and scalability evidence are insufficient. All environments are constructed SCMs, including the medically named PSA example. The large example adds redundant variables but retains only two POMPSes; it therefore does not test scaling with many genuinely competing scopes. POMPS enumeration costs, optimization runtime, and performance across diverse graph structures are not reported.

Several mathematical inconsistencies affect verification of the benchmarks. Appendix A.2 omits Cancer from the PSA equation but subsequently substitutes it to obtain the claimed sum-of-squares objective and zero optimum. Appendix C specifies the self-referential equation C4 ~ N(C4, 0.1). Section 5 defines regret as observed reward minus optimal expected reward, which has the wrong sign for the maximization experiments. These may be correctable errors, but the intended environments and plotted quantities must be made consistent.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the UCB rule and exploration settings, initialization, GP configuration, several intervention domains, and baseline implementation details are insufficiently specified. Although the conclusion states that code is shared, the supplied manuscript provides no repository link.
